entry: Hungarian composer, virtuoso pianist, conductor and teacher of the Romantic period. Liszt was a concert pianist from an early age, and his tours of Europe in the 1830s and 1840s brought him a degree of stardom known as "Lisztomania." He was a friend and promoter of composers including [[Hector Berlioz]], [[Frédéric Chopin]], [[Robert Schumann]], [[Clara Schumann]] and [[Richard Wagner]], and he was the first to apply the terms "transcription" and "paraphrase" to music. With Wagner he was a leading figure of the New German School. Liszt taught piano to hundreds of students and invented the masterclass as a method of teaching performance. He is credited with the symphonic poem and with innovations in thematic transformation, and his late works experimented with atonality. Today he is best known for his piano works, including the Hungarian Rhapsodies, the *Transcendental Études* and the Piano Sonata in B minor.

Austrian composer of the late Classical and early Romantic eras. Schubert was prolific despite a short life, leaving more than 1,000 compositions, including over 600 Lieder (art songs), seven complete symphonies, sacred music, operas and a large body of piano and chamber music. His best-known works include the songs "Gretchen am Spinnrade" and "Erlkönig," the *Trout Quintet*, and the song cycles *Die schöne Müllerin* and *Winterreise*. During his lifetime his music was appreciated mainly by a small circle in Vienna, and he gave only one concert of his works, in March 1828. After his death, [[Felix Mendelssohn]], [[Robert Schumann]], [[Franz Liszt]] and [[Johannes Brahms]] championed his music, and he is considered one of the greatest composers in the history of Western classical music.

American television sitcom broadcast on [[NBC]] from 1993 to 2004. A third spin-off and sequel to *Cheers*, it follows psychiatrist Frasier Crane, played by [[Kelsey Grammer]], who returns to [[Seattle]] to host a call-in radio show and takes in his retired police detective father. The series and its cast won 37 Primetime Emmy Awards, a record for a scripted series at the time. A revival premiered on Paramount+ in 2023.

Intentional deception to deprive a victim of a legal right or to gain from a victim unlawfully or unfairly. Fraud can be a civil wrong, in which a victim may sue to stop the fraud or recover money, or a [[Crime|criminal]] offense, for which the perpetrator may be prosecuted and imprisoned. In common law jurisdictions, civil fraud is a [[Tort|tort]] whose elements generally include an intentional misrepresentation or concealment of an important fact on which the victim relies to their detriment. Intent is the key element and is often difficult to prove. Fraud may also serve as a defense to a civil action for breach of [[Contract|contract]]. Criminal fraud takes many forms, including bank fraud, insurance fraud and forgery. Remedies for civil fraud include rescission of the transaction, [[Damages|damages]] and punitive damages. The purpose may be monetary gain or other benefits, such as obtaining a passport.

Genus of plants in the olive and lilac family, Oleaceae, commonly called ash. It comprises 45–65 species of usually medium-to-large trees, most of them deciduous, although some subtropical species are evergreen. The genus is widespread across Europe, Asia and North America. Its leaves are usually opposite and mostly pinnately compound, and its seeds, called "keys," are winged samaras. Ash wood is strong and elastic and is used for tool handles, and by instrument makers for [[Electric guitar|electric guitars]] and [[Drum|drum]] shells. In [[Greek mythology]], the Meliae were the nymphs of ash trees. The genus name comes from the [[Latin]] *frāxinus*, and the genus was described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753. The oldest clearly identified fossils are from the [[Eocene|Middle Eocene]] of southeastern North America.

American dancer, actor, singer and choreographer. Born Frederick Austerlitz in [[Omaha, Nebraska]], he performed as a child in a brother-and-sister act with his older sister Adele, a format common in [[Vaudeville|vaudeville]]. His dancing drew on tap, classical dance and the style of Vernon and Irene Castle, and it greatly influenced the American Smooth style of [[Ballroom dance|ballroom dance]]. He made a series of Hollywood musicals with [[Ginger Rogers]], including *Top Hat* (1935), *Swing Time* (1936) and *Shall We Dance* (1937). Later films included *Holiday Inn* (1942) and *The Band Wagon* (1953). For *The Towering Inferno* (1974) he received his only competitive Academy Award nomination, for Best Supporting Actor. He received an Honorary Academy Award in 1950, and his career across stage, film and television spanned 76 years. He was inducted into the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 1960.

American television host, Presbyterian minister and author. Rogers began his television career at [[NBC]] in New York City, then returned to [[Pittsburgh]] in 1953 to work on children's programming at WQED. He helped develop the children's series *Misterogers* for the [[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]] and became a Presbyterian minister in 1963. He created *Mister Rogers' Neighborhood*, which ran from 1968 to 2001 and addressed children's emotional concerns such as death, sibling rivalry, school enrollment and divorce. He received more than forty honorary degrees, a Lifetime Achievement Emmy in 1997 and the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2002. He was inducted into the Television Hall of Fame in 1999.

British rock singer and songwriter, lead vocalist of [[Queen (band)|Queen]]. Born in [[Zanzibar]] to [[Parsis|Parsi]] parents, he formed Queen in 1970 with Brian May and Roger Taylor and wrote hits including "Killer Queen," "Bohemian Rhapsody" and "We Are the Champions." His flamboyant stage presence and four-octave range shaped the band's live performances, and its 1985 set at [[Live Aid]] is often ranked among the greatest in rock history. He also pursued a solo career. He announced his AIDS diagnosis publicly the day before he died.

Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1155–1190) and German king of the Hohenstaufen dynasty. Frederick was elected king of Germany at [[Frankfurt]] in 1152 and crowned emperor by [[Pope]] Adrian IV in Rome in 1155. The nickname Barbarossa, "Red Beard" in Italian, was first used by Florentines in 1298. His Italian campaigns brought conquests such as [[Milan]], but a defeat at Legnano in 1176 led to reconciliation with the papacy and to the Peace of Constance (1183), which granted the Lombard cities autonomy. He joined the [[Third Crusade]] and drowned while crossing the Saleph River, after which most of his army abandoned the campaign. Historians rank him among the greatest medieval emperors of the [[Holy Roman Empire]], and his re-establishment of the [[Corpus Juris Civilis]] counterbalanced papal power. Later movements, including the Risorgimento and the Nazi movement, used him as a political symbol, with mixed results.

American social reformer, [[Abolitionism|abolitionist]], orator and writer. After escaping from slavery in Maryland in 1838, Douglass became a national leader of the abolitionist movement in Massachusetts and New York. His *Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave* (1845) became a bestseller and helped promote abolition. After the Civil War he campaigned for the rights of freed slaves and supported [[Women's suffrage|women's suffrage]]. He also advised [[Abraham Lincoln]] on emancipation. In 1872, without his knowledge or consent, he became the first African American nominated for vice president of the United States, as running mate of Victoria Woodhull on the Equal Rights Party ticket. When radical abolitionists criticized his willingness to deal with slaveholders, he replied: "I would unite with anybody to do right and with nobody to do wrong."

Holy Roman Emperor (r. 1220–1250), also King of Sicily, Germany and Jerusalem. He was the grandson of [[Frederick Barbarossa]] and son of Emperor Henry VI. Known as *Stupor mundi* ("Wonder of the World"), he viewed himself as a successor to the emperors of antiquity and ruled a realm stretching from Sicily through much of Italy to Germany. He was frequently at war with the papacy and was repeatedly excommunicated; Pope Innocent IV called him the forerunner of the [[Antichrist]]. He built an early absolutist state in the [[Kingdom of Sicily]] with an efficient secular bureaucracy. His court at [[Palermo]] was a cultural hub, and the Sicilian School of poetry helped shape the modern Italian language. He was the first monarch to formally outlaw trial by ordeal. The Treaty of Jaffa (1229) with Sultan al-Kamil regained [[Jerusalem]], [[Nazareth]] and [[Bethlehem]] for Christians while allowing Muslim access to holy sites. He has been called the greatest of all the German emperors.

American historian known for the frontier thesis. Turner taught at the University of Wisconsin until 1910, when he moved to [[Harvard University]], where he remained until 1922. He trained many doctoral students who became well-known historians, and he promoted interdisciplinary and quantitative methods, with an emphasis on the [[Midwestern United States]]. His essay "The Significance of the Frontier in American History" argued that the moving western frontier strongly shaped American democracy and character from the colonial era until 1890. Historians have argued over the thesis, but all agree it has had an enormous effect on historical scholarship. Turner earned his PhD at [[Johns Hopkins University]] in 1890 with a thesis on the fur trade in Wisconsin. By 1910 he was considered one of the two or three most influential historians in the country, and he also developed a theory of geographical sectionalism.

American landscape architect, considered the father of [[Landscape architecture|landscape architecture]] in the United States. Olmsted co-designed many urban parks with his partner Calvert Vaux, beginning with [[Central Park]] in New York City, and their work included Prospect Park in Brooklyn and a coordinated system of parks and parkways in [[Buffalo, New York|Buffalo]]. He created the Emerald Necklace in [[Boston]], designed one of the first planned communities in the United States at Riverside, Illinois, and drew master plans for the [[University of California, Berkeley|University of California, Berkeley]], [[Stanford University]] and the [[University of Chicago]]. He established his practice at Fairsted in Brookline, Massachusetts, in 1883, and his sons carried on the firm as Olmsted Brothers. During the Civil War he headed the U.S. Sanitary Commission, organizing medical services for the Union Army. He was also an early leader of the conservation movement, contributing to the preservation of [[Niagara Falls]].

British biochemist, twice a winner of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Sanger won the 1958 prize for determining the amino acid sequence of [[Insulin|insulin]] and other proteins, showing that each had a unique, definite structure, a foundational discovery for the central dogma of molecular biology. His insulin work used techniques including [[Chromatography|paper chromatography]]. At the Laboratory of Molecular Biology in [[Cambridge]], he developed the first DNA sequencing technique, which greatly expanded the experiments feasible in molecular biology. He shared the 1980 prize with Walter Gilbert and Paul Berg. He is one of only three people to win multiple Nobel Prizes in the same category, the others being [[John Bardeen]] in physics and Karl Barry Sharpless in chemistry. He was brought up as a [[Quakers|Quaker]].

King in [[Prussia]] and Elector of Brandenburg (r. 1713–1740), known as the Soldier King. Born in [[Berlin]], he became politically aware during the plague outbreak of the [[Great Northern War]], and an exposed embezzlement scandal convinced him to resist corruption and inefficiency. On his accession he dismissed his father's corrupt advisers and set out to reorganize the finances his father had ruined. He expanded the army from 38,000 men in 1713 to 80,000 in 1740, an average of 1 out of every 25 Prussian men serving, and replaced military service for the middle class with an annual tax. He also established schools and hospitals. An advocate of [[Absolute monarchy|absolute monarchy]], he centralized authority and was known for the Potsdam Giants, an elite guard of very tall soldiers. He was succeeded by his son, [[Frederick the Great]].

Monarch of [[Kingdom of Prussia|Prussia]] (r. 1740–1786) and the last Hohenzollern monarch titled King in Prussia. In his youth he was more interested in music and philosophy than war, and he clashed with his authoritarian father, [[Frederick William I of Prussia|Frederick William I]]. After taking the throne he seized the Austrian province of [[Silesia]] and became an influential military theorist. He defended Silesia in the [[Seven Years' War]]. A supporter of enlightened absolutism, he described the ruler as the first servant of the state. He modernized the bureaucracy and judiciary, allowed men of lower status to become judges, and tolerated Jews and Catholics while favoring Protestantism. He corresponded with [[Voltaire]] and supported the arts and philosophers. Prussia gained territory in the First Partition of Poland in 1772. He was succeeded by his nephew, Frederick William II. Nazi propaganda glorified him as a forerunner of [[Adolf Hitler]], who admired him, and his reputation in Germany became less favorable after World War II.

Creative work whose [[Copyright|copyright]] and other restrictions on use and modification are minimal. Free content, also called libre or open content, can be freely studied, applied, copied and modified by anyone for any purpose, including commercial use. It covers all works in the [[Public domain|public domain]] and works under licenses such as the [[Creative Commons]] CC BY, CC BY-SA and CC0 licenses. Under the Berne Convention, copyright applies by default, so an author must declare a work free, usually through a license statement.

Human right to practice, or not practice, a religion free from interference by government. Considered by most nations a fundamental human right, freedom of religion is protected by major conventions, including the [[International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights]]. It includes freedom of belief, covering [[Atheism|atheism]], [[Humanism|humanism]] and other forms of nonbelief, and some hold that it must also include freedom of practice. Courts often decide whether religious practices that break secular law should be permitted. In a country with a state religion, it generally means the government allows the practices of other faiths. The [[Statue of Liberty]] in New York, created to commemorate the abolition of slavery, later came to represent hope for religious refugees, and the [[Golden Temple]] in [[Amritsar]], India, symbolizes freedom of worship. In some countries, [[Apostasy|apostasy laws]] still punish religious conversion.

Right to communicate one's opinions and ideas without fear of retaliation, censorship or legal sanction. It is recognized as a human right in the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]] (UDHR) and protected by many national constitutions. Article 19 of the UDHR includes the freedom to seek, receive and impart information, but the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights allows restrictions for the rights or reputation of others and for national security, public order, public health or morals. Common limits include libel, incitement, hate speech, classified information and copyright violation. In *On Liberty*, [[John Stuart Mill]] proposed the harm principle, that power may rightly be exercised over members of a civilized community only to prevent harm to others. [[Erasmus]] and [[Voltaire]] championed free expression, and England's Bill of Rights of 1689 established parliamentary privilege. In the digital age, countries may use [[Internet|internet]] censorship, and social media platforms moderate content that breaches their terms of service, even when it is legal.

Group of fraternal organizations that trace their origins to medieval guilds of stonemasons. Freemasonry is considered the oldest existing secular fraternal organization, with documents dating to the 14th century. Its core tenets are brotherly love, relief and truth. The basic unit is the lodge, usually supervised by a Grand Lodge, and there is no worldwide Grand Lodge. The United Grand Lodge of England, dating to June 1717, is regarded as the mother Grand Lodge. Regular Freemasonry, the largest branch, requires that a volume of sacred law such as the [[Bible]] or the [[Quran]] be open in lodge, that members profess belief in a supreme being, and that women not be admitted. Liberal or Continental Freemasonry has removed some of these requirements. The [[Catholic Church]] and some Protestant denominations have opposed membership, and some Islamic countries have banned it. Opposition is sometimes rooted in [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]] or conspiracy theories. Enlightenment-era figures such as [[Benjamin Franklin]] and [[George Washington]] are associated with the movement.

Social movement espousing unorthodox beliefs formed independently of authority, tradition, revelation or dogma. Freethinkers hold that knowledge should be grounded in facts, scientific inquiry and logic, free from confirmation bias, prejudice and conventional wisdom. The term came into use in the 17th century for people who examined traditional beliefs. Today freethought is most closely linked with [[Agnosticism|agnosticism]], [[Deism|deism]], [[Secularism|secularism]], [[Humanism|humanism]] and religious critique. Freethinkers typically hold that there is insufficient evidence for supernatural phenomena. The British mathematician and philosopher William Kingdon Clifford's essay "The Ethics of Belief," published in the 1870s, argued that believing anything on insufficient evidence is always wrong, and it became a rallying cry for freethinkers. [[Bertrand Russell]] wrote that a freethinker is one whose beliefs rest on evidence rather than bias, and that atheists and agnostics are not necessarily freethinkers. Key historical figures include [[Voltaire]] and [[Thomas Paine]].

Capital and largest city of [[Sierra Leone]], a port on the [[Atlantic Ocean]] (pop., 2024: 1,347,559). It is the seat of the national government and the country's main urban, economic, educational and political center. Its economy centers on a harbor occupying part of the Sierra Leone River estuary, one of the world's largest natural deepwater harbors. Freetown was founded on March 11, 1792, by 1,196 [[African Americans|African Americans]] under the guidance of abolitionist John Clarkson, and it became a settlement for free and freed Black settlers. Their descendants, the Creole people, speak Krio, by far the most widely spoken language in the city. No single ethnic group forms more than 27% of the population.

Phase transition in which a liquid turns into a solid when cooled below its freezing point. For most substances the melting and freezing points are the same, though some, such as agar, show hysteresis. Most liquids freeze by crystallization, in which molecules gather into nanoscale clusters that arrange in a periodic crystal structure and then grow. Pure liquids can supercool below their freezing point until nucleation begins; [[Water|water]] can supercool to −40 °C in the absence of nucleators. Freezing is almost always exothermic, releasing latent heat. Low-temperature [[Helium-3|helium-3]] is the known exception, with a negative enthalpy of fusion below 0.3 K. Materials such as [[Glass|glass]] and [[Glycerol|glycerol]] harden into amorphous solids without a sharp freezing point. Water is unusual in expanding by about 9% when it freezes, and freezing is essential to [[Food preservation|food preservation]].

Physical process of transporting commercial goods and cargo, also called freight forwarding. Modes include air, water, rail, pipelines and road, with pipelines carrying liquids and gases. Early goods were carried by animals such as horses, [[Camel|camels]] and donkeys. The invention of the [[Wheel|wheel]] in [[Mesopotamia]] in 5000 BC allowed carts, and Silk Road trade moved goods by camel caravan. During the [[Industrial Revolution]], England's canal system and railways carried freight over long distances. After the [[Wright brothers]] invented the airplane, the first air freight shipment was delivered in 1910, and FedEx's founding in 1973 revolutionized the industry with specialized cargo flights. In 2015, 108 trillion tonne-kilometers were transported worldwide: 70% by sea, 18% by road, 9% by rail, 2% by inland waterways and under 0.25% by air. Merchant shipping carries 80–90% of international trade and 60–70% by value.

French breed of companion dog, also called the Frenchie. It appeared in Paris in the mid-nineteenth century, apparently from crossing Toy [[Bulldog|Bulldogs]] imported from England with local Parisian ratters. Lace workers from [[Nottingham]] who settled in [[Normandy]] brought small Bulldogs to France. The breed was fashionable among artists such as [[Edgar Degas]] and [[Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec]]. It is among the most frequently registered dogs in Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States. Its flat face and skin wrinkles make it prone to breathing and other health problems.
